manuscript_support: Absent from Sinaiticus (א) and Vaticanus (B); the oldest manuscripts end at 16:8. Supported by A, C, D, W, and the majority text. Eusebius and Jerome note its absence from most Greek manuscripts of their day.
explanation: The two oldest and most reliable Greek manuscripts end Mark's Gospel abruptly at 16:8 with the women fleeing in fear. Verses 9-20 include the appearances of the risen Jesus, the Great Commission, and the promise of signs (snake handling, speaking in tongues). Most scholars regard this section as a second-century addition to provide a more satisfying ending. The shorter ending and the 'Freer Logion' (in codex W) are also attested.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Mk 16:9; UBS5 rating: A (for ending at v.8)

short_title: The Woman Caught in Adultery (Pericope Adulterae)
manuscript_support: Absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and most early Greek manuscripts. Present in D (Codex Bezae) and the majority of later manuscripts. Some manuscripts place it after Luke 21:38 or at the end of John.
explanation: The story of Jesus forgiving the woman caught in adultery is absent from our earliest and best manuscripts of John. Its floating location in the manuscript tradition—appearing variously after John 7:52, John 21:25, or in Luke—strongly suggests it was a beloved oral tradition inserted into different Gospel contexts. Most scholars believe it preserves an authentic early Christian story even if it was not part of John's original text.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Jn 7:53; UBS5 rating: A (for omission)

manuscript_support: The phrase 'in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit' is absent from all Greek manuscripts before the 16th century except four late minuscules. Absent from the Latin Vulgate before the 6th century. Present only in a few Latin manuscripts from the 4th century onward, and in the Textus Receptus.
explanation: The Comma Johanneum—the only explicit Trinitarian formula in the NT ('the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one')—has virtually no support in the Greek manuscript tradition. It appears to have originated as a marginal gloss in Latin manuscripts commenting on the Trinity and was later incorporated into the text. It was included in Erasmus's third edition (1522) under pressure, and from there entered the KJV through the Textus Receptus.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on 1 Jn 5:7-8; UBS5 rating: A (for omission)

manuscript_support: The doxology 'For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen' is absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and other early manuscripts. Present in D, majority text, and the Didache (a late 1st-century church manual).
explanation: The familiar doxology ending the Lord's Prayer was not part of Matthew's original text. It appears to have been added in liturgical use—probably drawn from 1 Chronicles 29:11—as congregations naturally concluded the prayer with praise. The Didache shows it was in liturgical use very early, and scribes eventually incorporated it into the Gospel text. Most modern translations include it in brackets or a footnote.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Mt 6:13; UBS5 rating: A (for omission)

manuscript_support: Absent from P45, P74, Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and most reliable manuscripts. Present in E, many minuscules, and the Latin tradition. Irenaeus may have known a form of it in the 2nd century.
explanation: The verse containing Philip's question ('Do you believe with all your heart?') and the eunuch's confession ('I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God') is missing from the best manuscripts. It appears to be a liturgical addition, reflecting early baptismal practice where a confession was required before baptism. The verse gives the passage a more complete baptismal structure, which is probably why scribes added it.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Acts 8:37; UBS5 rating: A (for omission)

manuscript_support: Absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), P46, and other early manuscripts. Present in D, F, G, and the majority text. A duplicate of the benediction in 16:20b.
explanation: This verse ('The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen') is an apparent doublet of the benediction that appears in 16:20. Scribes who had manuscripts placing the doxology of 16:25-27 after chapter 14 left 16:20's benediction looking like a letter closing, prompting them to add another closing at 16:24 to round off the chapter.

manuscript_support: 'Son of God' is present in A, B², D, and most manuscripts, but absent from Sinaiticus (א*), Theta (Θ), and a few other witnesses. P46 does not cover this verse.
explanation: The phrase 'Son of God' at the very opening of Mark ('The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God') is absent from some significant manuscripts, including the original hand of Sinaiticus. Some scholars argue it was a later christological addition to Mark's opening, while others suggest it was accidentally omitted by scribes due to a homoioteleuton error (the Greek endings of 'Christ' and 'God' are similar). The UBS committee rates inclusion as probable but not certain.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Mk 1:1; UBS5 rating: B (probable inclusion)

manuscript_support: Absent from P75, Sinaiticus (א*), Vaticanus (B), and several other early manuscripts. Present in Sinaiticus (corrector), D, and the majority text. Cited by Justin Martyr and Irenaeus in the 2nd century.
explanation: The verses describing an angel strengthening Jesus and his sweat becoming 'like drops of blood' appear in some very early witnesses (Justin, Irenaeus) yet are absent from some of our best manuscripts. Some scholars believe they are authentic to Luke but were omitted by early scribes who found the picture of Jesus needing angelic support problematic for a high Christology. Others argue they were inserted from an early tradition. The UBS rates this as a difficult call.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Lk 22:43-44; UBS5 rating: B

short_title: The Angel Troubling the Water at Bethesda
manuscript_support: The end of verse 3 ('waiting for the moving of the water') and all of verse 4 (the angel stirring the pool) are absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and other early manuscripts. Present in A, C, and the majority text.
explanation: The explanation that an angel periodically stirred the pool and the first one in was healed is missing from the oldest manuscripts. It appears to be a scribal gloss added to explain why the paralyzed man in verse 7 mentions waiting for the water to be stirred—a detail that is otherwise unexplained for readers unfamiliar with local Jerusalem tradition. The note helpfully clarifies the story but was not part of John's original text.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Jn 5:3-4; UBS5 rating: A (for omission)

manuscript_support: Absent from P74, Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and many other manuscripts. Present in D (in an expanded form) and other Western text witnesses.
explanation: This verse, which says that Silas decided to stay at Antioch (despite verse 33 saying the delegation returned to Jerusalem), appears to be a harmonizing insertion. Without it, Silas is conveniently in Antioch for Paul to choose him as a companion in verse 40, which puzzles readers who noticed verse 33. A scribe added verse 34 to resolve the apparent inconsistency.

manuscript_support: The prayer 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing' is absent from P75, Sinaiticus (א*), Vaticanus (B*), D*, W, and other early witnesses. Present in the majority of later manuscripts and cited early by Irenaeus and others.
explanation: One of Jesus's most beloved sayings from the cross has surprisingly weak manuscript support. Several of our oldest and best manuscripts lack it. Some scholars suggest it was omitted by scribes who felt the prayer had not been answered (given the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD). Others argue it is an early addition drawn from the tradition of Stephen's prayer in Acts 7:60. The UBS committee was divided, giving it a C rating.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Lk 23:34; UBS5 rating: C (doubtful)

short_title: Only Begotten God vs. Only Begotten Son
manuscript_support: 'Only begotten God' (μονογενὴς θεός) is supported by P66, P75, Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and Origen. 'Only begotten Son' (μονογενὴς υἱός) is found in A, C, and the majority text, and was the more familiar reading in the early church.
explanation: The prologue of John ends with either 'the only begotten God' or 'the only begotten Son' (depending on your manuscript). The reading 'only begotten God' has stronger early support and is considered more difficult—scribes would have been more likely to change the theologically bold 'God' to the familiar Johannine phrase 'Son of God' than vice versa. Most modern translations follow the early manuscripts and read 'God.'
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Jn 1:18; UBS5 rating: B

manuscript_support: The longer form ('bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you') found in the majority text and the parallel in Luke 6:27-28 is absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and early papyri. The shorter form is widely regarded as original to Matthew.
explanation: Several manuscripts expand Jesus's command to 'love your enemies' with additional clauses drawn from Luke's parallel account ('bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, pray for those who mistreat you'). The best manuscripts support the shorter Matthean form. This is a classic case of scribal harmonization—scribes blended the two Gospel accounts to make them agree, creating a fuller-sounding but secondary text.

manuscript_support: The phrase 'who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit' at the end of 8:1 is absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and P46. Present in the majority text (copied from 8:4).
explanation: The great declaration 'There is therefore now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus' stands complete in the earliest manuscripts without qualification. The phrase that was later added—'who walk not after the flesh but after the Spirit'—appears to have been copied from verse 4, where it genuinely belongs. Most modern translations omit the addition, preserving the unconditional force of Paul's statement.

short_title: Women Silent in Churches — Location in Manuscripts
manuscript_support: In Codex D (Bezae) and several Western manuscripts, these verses appear after verse 40 rather than after verse 33. All manuscripts contain them, but their placement varies.
explanation: The verses commanding women to be silent in churches (14:34-35) appear in all manuscripts but in two different locations—after verse 33 in most manuscripts and after verse 40 in the Western tradition. Some scholars argue that the floating placement suggests they were originally a marginal gloss (perhaps drawn from 1 Tim 2:11-12) that was inserted into the text at different points by different scribes. Others maintain the verses are original and the transposition is secondary. This remains one of the more debated textual questions in Pauline studies.

manuscript_support: The words 'in Ephesus' are absent from P46, Sinaiticus (א*), and Vaticanus (B*). Origen knew manuscripts lacking the location. Present in the correctors of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and in the majority of manuscripts.
explanation: The words 'in Ephesus' may not have been in the original letter, suggesting Ephesians was a circular letter sent to multiple churches with a blank for the local destination. Marcion called it 'the letter to the Laodiceans.' Manuscripts lacking the location fit the letter's notably impersonal tone—Paul never names any individuals in Ephesians, surprising for a church he spent three years with. The letter may have been intended as a general letter to Asia Minor churches.

manuscript_support: Verses 44 and 46 ('where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched') are absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and other early manuscripts. Present in the majority text. Verse 48 is genuine and contains the same language.
explanation: The vivid description of hell from Isaiah 66:24 appears three times in Mark 9 (vv. 44, 46, 48) in the KJV, but the oldest manuscripts only support the final occurrence in verse 48. Scribes apparently repeated the refrain after verses 43 and 45 by analogy, creating a more symmetrical and emphatic threefold structure. Modern translations omit verses 44 and 46 or place them in brackets.

manuscript_support: The longer Matthean form of the Lord's Prayer found in some manuscripts of Luke 11:2-4 is absent from P75, Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B). The majority text shows various expansions toward the more familiar Matthew 6 version.
explanation: Luke's shorter, simpler Lord's Prayer was frequently expanded by scribes to match the more familiar and liturgically-used version in Matthew 6. Most additions are absent from the oldest manuscripts of Luke. This is a clear example of how liturgical use shaped the manuscript tradition—scribes and communities who knew the longer prayer by heart naturally incorporated it into their copies of Luke.

manuscript_support: Codex Bezae (D) consistently provides a longer, more expanded text of Acts throughout—often 8-10% longer than the Alexandrian text represented by P74, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus.
explanation: The 'Western text' of Acts, best represented by Codex Bezae, contains numerous additional phrases, speeches, and narrative details not found in the earlier Alexandrian manuscripts. Scholars debate whether this represents an early alternative edition of Acts or the result of extensive second-century scribal expansion. Most critical editions follow the shorter Alexandrian text as more original, treating Western additions as variants of interest.
external_ref: NA28 Introduction on the Western text of Acts

short_title: Who is in Heaven — Expanded Phrase
manuscript_support: The phrase 'who is in heaven' at the end of John 3:13 ('the Son of Man who is in heaven') is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus (א), and Vaticanus (B). Present in the majority text.
explanation: The statement that the Son of Man is 'in heaven' even while Jesus is speaking on earth was a theologically rich phrase that may have been added to emphasize Christ's divine omnipresence or heavenly origin. The oldest manuscripts lack it. Whether original or added, the phrase reflects the high Christology of the Johannine tradition—the Son of Man simultaneously on earth and in heaven.

manuscript_support: Absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), P45, and other early manuscripts. Present in the majority text, copied from the parallel in Mark 9:29.
explanation: The saying 'But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting' is missing from the best manuscripts of Matthew 17 but does appear in Mark 9:29 (though even there, 'and fasting' is a later addition to Mark). This is a straightforward case of cross-Gospel harmonization—scribes familiar with the Markan parallel added it to Matthew to fill what seemed like a gap in Jesus's answer.

short_title: Matthew 18:11 — Son of Man Came to Save the Lost
manuscript_support: Absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), L, θ, and other early manuscripts. Present in D, the majority text. Copied from Luke 19:10.
explanation: The statement 'For the Son of Man came to save what was lost' is absent from the earliest Matthew manuscripts. It was inserted from the parallel in Luke 19:10, where it appears in context with the Zacchaeus story. In Matthew 18, its presence between the parables of the lost sheep and the offending brother seemed fitting to scribes, prompting harmonization with Luke.

manuscript_support: The clause 'it will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town' is absent from Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and other early manuscripts. Present in D and the majority text, drawn from Matthew 10:15.
explanation: The Sodom and Gomorrah comparison in Jesus's mission instructions appears in Matthew 10:15 but not in the earliest manuscripts of the parallel in Mark 6:11. Scribes who knew the fuller Matthean form of the missionary discourse added it to Mark. This is another example of the pervasive scribal tendency to harmonize the Synoptic Gospels with each other.

manuscript_support: Absent from Codex Bezae (D) and a few Latin witnesses. Present in P75, Sinaiticus (א), Vaticanus (B), and the majority of manuscripts.
explanation: The verse describing Peter running to the tomb and finding only the linen wrappings is absent from Codex Bezae. Some Western text critics argued it was a later insertion from John 20:3-10. However, its presence in P75 and the best Alexandrian manuscripts, along with its distinctive Lukan vocabulary, suggests it is original and that Bezae's omission is the secondary reading.

manuscript_support: The phrase 'and was carried up into heaven' is absent from Sinaiticus (א*), D, and several other witnesses. Present in P75, Vaticanus (B), and the majority text. The Western text also lacks 'and he was carried up' in Acts 1:2 in some witnesses.
explanation: The explicit statement that Jesus 'was carried up into heaven' in Luke 24:51 is missing from some early manuscripts. Its absence creates a version of Luke that ends only with Jesus blessing the disciples and departing—without the explicit ascension. Given that Luke-Acts is a two-volume work, the ascension narrative in Acts 1 is unambiguous, but the textual question here touches on how Luke narrated the end of his first volume.

manuscript_support: The doxology of Romans 16:25-27 appears after 14:23 in some manuscripts (including P, a number of Western witnesses, and some lectionaries), after chapter 15 in a few, and after chapter 16 in most. P46 has it after both 15:33 and 16:23.
explanation: The doxology that closes Romans ('Now to him who is able to strengthen you…') appears at different points in different manuscripts, reflecting the circulation of Romans in different lengths (a 14-chapter, 15-chapter, and 16-chapter form). Marcion appears to have used a short form ending at chapter 14. The varying location of the doxology is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that Romans circulated as a form letter with chapters 15-16 added for the Roman audience.

short_title: Apart from God vs. By the Grace of God
manuscript_support: 'Apart from God' (χωρὶς θεοῦ) is found in a few significant witnesses including Origen and a marginal reading in several manuscripts. 'By the grace of God' (χάριτι θεοῦ) is in the overwhelming majority of manuscripts including P46, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus.
explanation: A fascinating variant in Hebrews 2:9 debates whether Jesus tasted death 'by the grace of God' or 'apart from God.' The reading 'apart from God' (found in a small number of witnesses) would echo Jesus's cry of dereliction ('My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?') and has been championed by some scholars as the harder reading. The majority reading 'by the grace of God' has overwhelming manuscript support. The UBS committee retained 'by the grace of God' with a B rating.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Heb 2:9; UBS5 rating: B

short_title: God Was Manifest vs. He Who Was Manifest
manuscript_support: 'God was manifest in the flesh' (θεὸς ἐφανερώθη) is found in later manuscripts. 'He who was manifest in the flesh' (ὃς ἐφανερώθη) or simply 'which was manifest' is supported by Sinaiticus (א), A*, C*, and other early manuscripts. The difference in Greek is between ΟΣ (who) and ΘΣ (God—a scribal abbreviation).
explanation: The KJV reads 'God was manifest in the flesh'—a powerful Trinitarian proof text—but this depends on a difference of only two letters in Greek (the nomen sacrum ΘΣ for 'God' versus ΟΣ for 'who'). The older manuscripts support 'who' or 'which.' Most scholars believe a scribe altered the relative pronoun into the abbreviation for 'God' to clarify the theology, giving us one of the KJV's most explicitly Trinitarian verses that was not in the original text.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on 1 Tim 3:16; UBS5 rating: A (for 'who')

short_title: Son of God vs. Chosen One of God
manuscript_support: 'The Son of God' is found in the majority of manuscripts. 'The Chosen One of God' (ὁ ἐκλεκτὸς τοῦ θεοῦ) is supported by P5, P106, Sinaiticus (א*), and the Old Latin tradition.
explanation: John the Baptist's declaration at Jesus's baptism may have originally called Jesus 'the Chosen One of God' rather than 'the Son of God.' The 'Chosen One' reading connects powerfully to Isaiah's servant songs ('my chosen one in whom I delight') and to the transfiguration accounts. Some scholars prefer it as the harder reading, since scribes would more easily change the unique 'Chosen One' to the familiar 'Son of God' than vice versa.
external_ref: NA28 apparatus on Jn 1:34; UBS5 rating: B

manuscript_support: A 'shorter ending' ('And all that had been commanded them they told briefly to those around Peter. After this, Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the holy and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation.') appears in some manuscripts (L, Ψ, 099, 0112, and several others) after 16:8, sometimes alongside the Long Ending.
explanation: Some manuscripts that recognized that Mark 16:8 was an unsatisfying ending added a brief concluding paragraph before (or instead of) the Long Ending, summarizing the mission of the disciples. This shorter ending is clearly secondary—its vocabulary and style differ markedly from Mark. Its existence, along with the Long Ending, shows that scribes from the 2nd century onward felt compelled to give Mark a more complete conclusion.
